newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lead premiums perk up, relishing heat waves.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lead premiums perk up, relishing heat waves.

text.p: Spot lead premiums in the United States have begun to perk up as the summer battery season approaches, with hopes that heat waves in New York and elsewhere will boost demand after a dull winter, dealers and analysts said.

"Lead premiums have been quite active - on the physical side things seem to be picking up in the U.S.," a merchant said. "The heat waves in certain parts of the country will certainly have an impact on demand for lead."
Very hot weather kills lead-acid auto starter batteries quicker than cold weather, dealers noted.
Last winter was disappointing for the lead industry because fewer batteries failed in the mild winter.
"The battery companies are starting to gear up, they are buying for the summer battery making season," David Cook of Lake Engineering said.
"This hot weather is getting them to think they might have a pretty good second half of the year as far as replacement batteries," Cook added.
One lead recycling official said the market has reached the very bottom of the seasonal slowdown as battery makers take summer vacations.
"Are we seeing any pick up now? No. But do we anticipate the market picking up soon? Yes," the official added.
Lead premiums have jumped from a low of 1.5 cents to a new range of 2.5 to 3.00 cents a lb, dealers said.
Premiums on metal have firmed as primary smelters are largely sold out, and secondary production is weaker.
Meanwhile battery scrap prices have eased off about a cent to 6.5 to 7.5 cents a lb delivered.
"The tightness has decreased a good bit and the flow has picked up substantially," a second lead recycler said.
The voracious Mexican appetite for U.S. battery scrap, which helped push up domestic prices, has also abated for now at least, the recycler added.
Secondary lead producer RSR Corp has one furnace down for scheduled maintenance until the end of the month at Indianapolis, but the company had been stockpiling metal to keep shipments steady.
"I expect to see another cent or two increase (in premiums) before it's over and we start getting more scrap from the summer battery season to bring premiums down," Cook said.
